case_study_insert.main_stem: Greenvale Dairy Cooperative (GDC) is a cooperative in the dairy processing sector, employing a workforce of 120. Founded in 1998 by the Greenvale valley farmers' group and led by chairperson Rosa Delgado, it supplies cheese and fresh milk to regional supermarket chains across the valley, using a hierarchical structure with autocratic plant management. GDC plans to invest $1,400,000 in a new automated cheese-packing and cold-storage facility, financed by an $800,000 member share issue and a $600,000 bank loan. It has fixed costs of $420,000 a year, a variable cost of $7.70 a unit and a selling price of $14.70, and currently produces 150,000 units a year. GDC suffers repeated cold-chain failures and rising labour turnover on the packing floor.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Cold-chain Report — October 2026: The packing plant processed 37,500 units last quarter at a defect rate of 2.1%, down from 3.4% a year ago. Cold-chain failures caused 14 rejected consignments this year, down from 29 in 2025, and customer complaints fell from 33 to 19 per month. A survey of 150 farmer-members found 72% support the automated packing expansion and 55% want investment in renewable-energy solar panels. Average delivery time to regional distributors is 4.5 days. Off-the-job cold-chain certification at the food institute costs $850 per employee; 26 of 120 staff lack up-to-date certification, while on-the-job coaching on the new packers continues.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Greenvale Dairy Cooperative as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.0% to 4.75%, raising borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.0% from $12.10 to $12.83 per hour from April 2026, increasing wage bills across agriculture and processing. (3) Feed and packaging input costs have risen 11.0% year-on-year, food-price inflation is running at 6.5%, while consumer spending on cheese grew 4.2% in the same period.

questions.question_text: GDC plans to fund part of its new automated cheese-packing and cold-storage facility with a member share issue. Explain two advantages for GDC of using a member share issue to fund the expansion instead of a bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A member share issue raises permanent capital from the 150 surveyed farmer-members and other cooperative members without any repayment schedule or interest charge, unlike the alternative of a larger bank loan. This protects GDC's cash flow while it already services a $600,000 loan and carries fixed costs of $420,000 a year, and it avoids the risk of the bank imposing restrictive covenants on the new cold-storage facility or on how the farmer-members are paid for their milk.

Point 2: A member share issue strengthens member commitment and loyalty, since farmers who buy shares have a direct stake in the cooperative's success and are more likely to supply milk consistently and support the automated packing project. It also avoids pledging the new $1,400,000 facility as collateral, so member equity absorbs the risk instead of the bank doing so, and it keeps decision-making within the cooperative's own democratic governance rather than passing control to an external lender with fixed interest and principal demands.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual analysis linked to GDC's cooperative structure and expansion.

questions.question_text: GDC is launching its new vintage cheddar to regional supermarkets. Consider television advertising, in-store supermarket tasting promotions, or sponsorship of the annual Greenvale valley farmers' fair. Which should GDC choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Television advertising: A regional TV campaign would build fast awareness of GDC's vintage cheddar across all the supermarket chains it supplies and reach millions of households quickly. However, production and airtime are expensive for a cooperative, much of the audience would be outside the Greenvale valley catchment, and the message would be fleeting. For a member-owned business funding a $1,400,000 facility through an $800,000 share issue, heavy TV spend could strain cash flow before the new cheese has proven itself on shelf.

In-store supermarket tasting promotions: Tastings put the cheddar directly in front of shoppers at the moment of purchase, let staff explain the cooperative story and the 72% member support for the expansion, and generate immediate trial and sales data per store. Costs are moderate and targeted, though reach is limited to participating stores and the effect fades once the promotion ends.

Sponsorship of the Greenvale valley farmers' fair: Sponsoring the fair reinforces GDC's local farmer-heritage brand, delights the 150 farmer-members, and reaches a loyal regional audience cheaply with strong goodwill and media coverage. Its weakness is scale: the fair reaches a few thousand people once a year, which cannot move the volume needed to justify a $1,400,000 automated packing facility supplying national supermarket chains, and non-attendees never see the product.

Recommendation: GDC should choose in-store supermarket tasting promotions. They convert shoppers at the point of sale where the cheese is stocked, cost far less than television, target precisely the consumers buying in the partner supermarkets, and generate measurable sales uplift and feedback. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a cooperative with a $600,000 bank loan to service, and the farmers' fair is rejected as too small and too occasional to build the volumes the new facility requires; GDC can keep the fair sponsorship as low-cost community goodwill alongside the tastings.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of GDC with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of GDC with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and the farmers' fair are rejected.

questions.question_text: GDC faces rising labour turnover on the packing floor and repeated cold-chain failures. Explain two benefits for GDC of introducing democratic participation in its packing department.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic participation, such as worker briefings and suggestion schemes on the packing floor, gives the 120 staff a voice in how shifts, cold-chain checks and machine loading are organised. This satisfies esteem and belonging needs, raises job satisfaction and can directly reduce labour turnover, cutting the cost of recruiting and retraining packers and reducing disruption to the 4.5-day delivery promise to regional distributors.

Point 2: Involving operators surfaces practical fixes from the people who run the cold chain daily, such as earlier temperature checks and faster fault reporting. This lowers the 2.1% defect rate further and prevents rejected consignments like the 14 cold-chain failures this year, protecting GDC's reputation with 72% of farmer-members who support the expansion and preserving the flow of 37,500 units per quarter through the plant. In combination, the two benefits attack both the attendance problem behind labour turnover and the process problem behind consignment rejections.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual analysis linked to GDC's turnover, cold-chain failures and quality.

questions.question_text: GDC wants to motivate its packing-floor workers and cut labour turnover. Consider introducing piece-rate bonus pay or a profit-sharing scheme across the cooperative. Which should GDC choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Piece-rate bonus pay: Paying packers per unit packed rewards individual effort directly and links pay to the 37,500 units processed per quarter, which can raise output speed and lower unit labour costs. It suits measurable, repetitive packing work and is easy to administer. However, it can push packers to rush, raising the 2.1% defect rate and worsening cold-chain handling, it can create friction between fast and careful workers, and it ignores quality, safety and teamwork — dangerous in a cold-storage environment handling dairy products with strict hygiene rules.

Profit-sharing scheme: Distributing a share of cooperative profits to all 120 staff rewards collective performance, aligns workers with member and customer interests, and reinforces the cooperative ethos that defines GDC. It encourages teamwork, quality and careful handling, which would protect the falling defect rate and the 4.5-day delivery record. Drawbacks are that individual effort is diluted across 120 people, payouts depend on annual profits rather than daily behaviour, and poor years (for example after 14 rejected consignments) could demotivate if nothing is paid.

Decision: GDC should choose the profit-sharing scheme. It fits the cooperative model, promotes the teamwork and care needed to eliminate cold-chain failures and the 2.1% defect rate, and benefits all 120 staff rather than penalising slower, careful workers. Piece-rate pay is rejected as too narrow and too likely to inflate defects and rejections, which would cost far more than the bonuses paid; GDC can review piece-rate elements only after certification is complete and quality stabilises. A clear communication plan and termly profit statements will be essential so all 120 staff understand how the scheme works.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two motivators with limited application to GDC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both motivators in the context of GDC.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both motivators in the context of GDC with a well-justified decision covering quality, turnover, cooperative structure and cost.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how GDC's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $420,000 ÷ ($14.70 − $7.70) = $420,000 ÷ $7.00 = 60,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 60,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $14.70 − $7.70 = $7.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $7.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways GDC's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. GDC's managers can compare the 60,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 150,000 units to confirm the cooperative is comfortably profitable, with a margin of safety of 90,000 units, informing whether the new automated facility can be run at full capacity and whether farmer-members can be paid a better milk price.
2. Contribution per unit of $7.00 lets managers model discounts negotiated with supermarket chains, for example a 10% price cut to $13.23 would drop contribution to $5.53, letting them judge whether the extra volume from a national listing would still cover the $420,000 fixed costs and the $600,000 bank loan.
3. Knowing fixed costs of $420,000 helps managers set the volume targets used to check the facility can service the $600,000 bank loan and decide when the $800,000 member share issue proceeds should be drawn down, protecting the 4.5-day delivery promise to distributors.
4. Managers can use unit cost data ($420,000 ÷ 150,000 units + $7.70 = $10.50 a unit) to benchmark performance across quarters, find waste driving the 14 rejected cold-chain consignments, and decide whether to renegotiate the $7.70 variable cost with feed and packaging suppliers amid the 11.0% input-cost inflation.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 60,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $7.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained in detail: First, GDC's managers can compare the 60,000-unit break-even output with the actual 150,000-unit run, confirming a margin of safety of 90,000 units and giving confidence to run the new automated facility at full capacity and even raise the milk price paid to farmer-members. Second, the $7.00 contribution per unit lets managers model discounts requested by supermarket chains — a 10% cut to $13.23 leaves just $5.53 per unit, so any volume deal must still cover the $420,000 fixed costs and the $600,000 bank loan service. Third, knowing fixed costs of $420,000 and contribution per unit supports checks that the facility can service the $600,000 bank loan and guides the drawdown timing of the $800,000 member share issue for the $1,400,000 automated packing and cold-storage project. Fourth, unit-cost benchmarking ($420,000 ÷ 150,000 units + $7.70 = $10.50 a unit) gives a quarterly yardstick to expose waste behind the 14 rejected cold-chain consignments and to challenge feed and packaging suppliers amid the 11.0% input-cost inflation.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate GDC's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has GDC's financial position improved? Which of the two ratios gives the stronger evidence, and why? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.42 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.37 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.74 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.65 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $260,000 inventories + $210,000 trade receivables + $70,000 cash = $540,000; 2025 current assets = $310,000 + $240,000 + $40,000 = $590,000. CR 2024 = $540,000 ÷ $380,000 current liabilities = 1.42; CR 2025 = $590,000 ÷ $430,000 = 1.37. AT 2024 = ($540,000 − $260,000) ÷ $380,000 = $280,000 ÷ $380,000 = 0.74; AT 2025 = ($590,000 − $310,000) ÷ $430,000 = $280,000 ÷ $430,000 = 0.65.

Evaluation: Liquidity has weakened. Current assets did rise from $540,000 to $590,000, but current liabilities rose faster, from $380,000 to $430,000, so short-term coverage slipped from 1.42 to 1.37. The AT line, excluding inventories, fell from 0.74 to 0.65, meaning GDC relies even more heavily on selling perishable dairy stock and collecting receivables to meet immediate debts. Cash fell sharply from $70,000 to $40,000, inventories climbed from $260,000 to $310,000 (risking spoilage in a 4.5-day delivery chain), and trade receivables increased from $210,000 to $240,000. Meanwhile the new $1,400,000 facility will add further cash demands on top of the $600,000 bank loan, so the cooperative should not interpret the share issue as a licence to relax working capital discipline. Which ratio gives the stronger evidence? The acid test is the stronger indicator of GDC's short-term solvency because it excludes inventories — perishable dairy stock that may need to be discounted or scrapped to realise cash — and it fell from 0.74 to 0.65, confirming that the weakening is driven by rising liabilities and falling cash rather than by any improvement in stock quality.

Conclusion: GDC's financial position has not improved. Both the CR (1.42 to 1.37) and the AT (0.74 to 0.65) show weaker short-term solvency, with cash falling to just $40,000. Before the expansion proceeds, GDC should tighten credit control on its $240,000 of receivables, cut perishable inventories, and agree staged drawdown of the member share issue rather than upfront spending.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables, cash and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether GDC's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for GDC of installing solar panels to power its cold-storage facility.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Solar panels would cut the electricity bill of running the cold-storage rooms around the clock, protecting the $7.70 variable cost per unit against volatile energy prices and reinforcing GDC's green credentials with the 55% of farmer-members who want renewable-energy investment. Lower running costs would help margins on the $14.70 cheese, strengthen the case for the $1,400,000 automated facility, and appeal to supermarket buyers who increasingly demand sustainable suppliers.

Disadvantage: Solar installation requires significant upfront capital at a time when GDC already plans $1,400,000 of expansion funded by an $800,000 member share issue and a $600,000 bank loan, risking overstretching cash when the 2025 position shows only $40,000 of cash on hand. The panels could take many years to recoup their cost in cloudy valley weather, maintenance and panel cleaning add recurring costs, and roof or land space at the plant may be limited by the cold-storage build itself, delaying the energy savings that were supposed to protect the $7.70 variable cost.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to GDC's facility, member priorities and finance.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 4.75%, the 6.0% minimum wage increase and the 11.0% rise in feed and packaging input costs will affect GDC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.0% to 4.75%): If GDC's $600,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75% rise adds about $4,500 a year in interest, a modest sum against fixed costs of $420,000 and the $1,400,000 facility budget. Higher rates would, however, raise the cost of any further borrowing and may encourage the cooperative to delay drawdown of the loan, and they could dampen consumer spending growth on cheese beyond the current 4.2%. The direct cash impact is small and can be managed by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (6.0%, to $12.83 per hour): The insert gives a 6.0% rise from $12.10 to $12.83 — a derived delta of $0.73 per hour ($12.83 − $12.10; check: 6.0% × $12.10 ≈ $0.73). Many of the 120 staff hold production and packing roles whose pay is anchored to the floor, and bands above the floor typically shift too. The insert does not state hours worked, so the annual cash impact cannot be computed precisely; however, every hour worked becomes more expensive from April 2026, making this a direct hit to the operating margin that would pressure the pay of farmer-members relative to staff, and would require productivity gains — such as the automation in the new facility, which should cut labour demand per unit — to offset it without raising the $14.70 selling price.

Input cost inflation (11.0% feed and packaging): Feed drives the milk price GDC pays its farmer-members and packaging covers the new facility's output. The insert gives a $7.70 variable cost per unit and an 11.0% year-on-year rise in these inputs. Taking the entire variable cost as an upper bound: 11.0% × $7.70 = about $0.85 per unit; at 150,000 units a year that is roughly $127,500 a year (150,000 × $0.85, derivation shown; an upper bound since not all of the $7.70 is feed and packaging). Even a fraction of that bound would erode the $7.00 contribution per unit and squeeze the margin available to pay members for their milk, so feed and packaging contracts should be renegotiated before the new facility comes online.

Conclusion: The minimum wage increase will have the greatest impact. It is a mechanical $0.73-per-hour ($12.83 − $12.10) rise with no cap on the hours worked across the 120-strong workforce, whereas the input-cost rise is bounded at roughly $127,500 a year as an explicit upper bound (in practice far less), and vastly more than the $4,500 interest increase. It directly pressures the cooperative's ability to retain and motivate 120 staff while turnover is already rising. GDC must therefore prioritise productivity from automation, careful shift planning and, only if needed, modest cheese price rises, while fixing the loan rate and renegotiating feed contracts to contain the smaller input and interest-rate risks.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to GDC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on GDC's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of GDC with a well-justified judgement that the minimum wage increase has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
